To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the brain microvessles take up glutamate with a Km of about 3 microM and a Vmax of about 10 nmol/mg protein/min.
isolated rat brain microvascular endothelial cells take up glutamate in a high-affinity, saturable manner.

the brain capillary endothelial cells possess a high-affinity transport system for glutamate, which may play a role in the maintenance of low levels of extracellular glutamate in the central nervous system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the blood-brain transport of glutamate.
the study of transport processes across the blood-brains barrier.
understanding the mechanism of glutamate transport across the blood-brains barrier.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the capillary endothelium of brain microvessles has the capability to actively take up glutamate from the interstitial space and that this process is a major contributor to the maintenance of low interstitial concentrations of glutamate.
the brain capillary transport system is capable of maintaining the low extracellular concentration of glutamate in brain tissue by removing glutamate from the extracellular space.

we have shown that the capillaries of the brain possess a high-affinity, energy-dependent, Na+-dependent glutamate transport system that may function in the unidirectionally outward transport of glutate from brain to blood.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the capillary uptake system is highly specific, taking up glutamate with a Km of 2 microM, and is not significantly affected by the presence of other amino acids.
the brain microvessle is capable of taking up glutamate in a highly efficient manner.
capillaries in the brain are not just a passive barrier between the blood and brain but are actively involved in the regulation of the chemical environment of the brain.
